title: Managers Who Bring Their Style Along
text:
Economists often treated corporate executives as interchangeable: put any capable manager in the same company and you should get roughly the same decisions. In 2003 Marianne Bertrand and Antoinette Schoar tested that view with a simple idea. They followed top managers who had moved between large American companies over several decades, and asked whether a manager's arrival changed a company's policies in a way that matched what that same manager had done before.

It did. Individual managers carried recognizable styles with them. Some consistently invested more, made more acquisitions, or took on more debt; others paid more dividends, held more cash or cut costs more aggressively. These personal differences explained a meaningful share of the variation in company policies, beyond what the company and the year would predict, and they were linked to differences in company performance.

The researchers also found that certain backgrounds predicted styles. For example, managers from older generations tended to be more conservative, while those with an MBA tended to follow more aggressive strategies.
lesson: A leader's personal habits and beliefs leave a lasting mark on an organization. Know your own style and its biases, and choose leaders whose style fits what you need.
source: Bertrand, M., and Schoar, A. (2003). Managing with style: The effect of managers on firm policies. Quarterly Journal of Economics, 118(4), 1169-1208.
caveat: Managers do not move between firms at random, so the results are strong evidence but not a perfect experiment.
